2. `c2_legal_admin_narrow`: Under the **2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading**, does the study examine (or plausibly examine on full text) a legal, administrative, regulatory, tenure/documentation, tariff/cost-recovery/subsidy, discretion/accommodation, enforcement/disconnection, or utility-ownership/regulatory-structure mechanism governing service access? evidence_quotes.quote: Assessing water resources adaptive capacity to climate change impacts in the Pacific Northwest Region of North America

The PNW is endowed with extensive water resources infrastructure and well-established and well-funded management agencies responsible for ensuring that water resources objectives (such as water supply, water quality, flood control, hydropower production, environmental services, etc.) are met.

Institutional barriers include systematic loss of technical capacity in many water resources agencies following the dam building era, jurisdictional fragmentation affecting response to drought, disconnections between water policy and practice, and entrenched bureaucratic resistance to change in many water management agencies.

raw_response.plain_vs_narrow_note: Although the abstract discusses institutional barriers, jurisdictional fragmentation and water allocation/operating rules under a broad governance reading, the paper fails Criterion 1, Criterion 3 and Criterion 4 because it is a non-empirical regional assessment of basin-level water resources climate adaptation rather than household or community water or sanitation service access; thus both decisions are exclude.
raw_response.rationale: This paper examines regional basin-scale water resources management and institutional adaptive capacity to hydrological climate change impacts (snowpack loss, streamflow shifts, flood control, hydropower, environmental services and bulk water allocation) in the Pacific Northwest. It does not study household or community water or sanitation service access (E07), presents an analytical perspective rather than primary empirical research or a systematic review, and measures institutional climate adaptation capacity rather than household/community service access outcomes.
